newsitem.title: USA: Court overturns part of Astra suit.
newsitem.headline: Court overturns part of Astra suit.

text.p: A U.S. appeals court Friday dismissed part of an injunction against Astra USA, which had prohibited the firm from enforcing settlement agreements with employees who alleged they were victims of sexual harassment.

Astra USA, a unit of Swedish pharmaceutical giant Astra AB, had asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit in August to overturn a lower court's ruling, which the company said could open it to lawsuits in connection to allegations of sexual harassment.

Astra entered cash settlement agreements, ranging from $20,000 to $100,000, with at least 11 employees who claimed they were victims of or witnessed sexual harassment, court documents said. The agreements prohibited the employees from filing charges against Astra with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission -- or helping other employees who wished to file charges.

The EEOC sued Astra, and argued in court that the provisions of the settlement interfered with three investigations into allegations of sexual harassment at the company and were contrary to public policy.

Astra lawyers said employees were told they should cooperate with the EEOC investigation into allegations of widespread sexual harassment at the company. But, they argued, the provision in the settlement prohibiting employees from filing further charges against Astra allowed the company to put the allegations behind it and should stand.
A U.S. District Court judge in Worcester, Mass. in late June barred Astra "from entering into or enforcing" both parts of the settlement.

Then in court records released Friday, the U.S. Court of Appeals said that the settlement did not prevent employees from cooperating with the EEOC investigation, but that those who entered into the deal could not file charges.

"The only issue we were concerned about had to do with whether the employees could file new charges. And we were pleased with the decision," said Benjamin Kincannon, a spokesman for Astra. "Having a non-filing provision in settlement agreements is the only way of bringing closure."
Predictably, the EEOC claimed victory also.

"In the facts of this case, the court says we don't need it (the filing provision). We still have a quarrel with these kind of agreements and ultimately I think it is an issue that will be revisited either in this case or another case," said Lou Graziano, trial attorney with the EEOC.

Astra USA, based in Westborough, Mass., fired its chief executive on June 26, alleging he engaged in "improper behaviour". The company also fired one other senior executive and two others resigned as a result of a sexual harassment scandal.

More than half a dozen former employees filed lawsuits against Astra and its senior executives, arguing that the chief executive and others sexually harassed employees and intimidated those who protested.
